newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: INTERVIEW - Ivorian power firm boss targets steady.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ivorian power firm boss targets steady.

text.p: The head of Ivory Coast's electricity company CIE, back in profit after privatisation, says further expansion of the sector will depend on the ability of the country and its citizens to pay.

Marcel Zadi Kessy predicted that Ivory Coast, which became self-sufficient in electricity in 1995 thanks mainly to the discovery of cheap off-shore gas, would expand electricity exports to its neighbours.
But he said the government and the industry were aware that gas was a one-off bonus and that they would have to rely on other sources of power in the longer term.
"A service never comes free," Zadi, chairman and managing director of both the CIE and the West African nation's water utility SODECI, told Reuters in an interview.
He said future expansion of the electricity sector within Ivory Coast depended on the growth of the Ivorian economy and the capacity of Ivorians to pay.
"The thought is there but that depends on the development of our country," he said in his eighth-floor office overlooking the lagoon in the commercial capital Abidjan.
"The problem is not so much one of construction, the techniques of construction are not a problem. It's the capacity to absorb the investment, to repay. There must be a market."
He said Ivorians themselves held the key to development of the sector. "Ivorians must make money, they must work hard and make money. Then they will have access to all the services."
CIE, privatised in 1990, manages the production and supply of electricity on behalf of the government.
It is 49 percent Ivorian owned and 51 percent owned by SAUR International, a subsidiary of French company Bouygues, and French power company Electricite de France.
The government, which calls the policy shots, manages the debt and handles major investment projects in the sector. It is also the main beneficiary of profits on electricity exports.
"We are an instrument of the state. We are paid for the service that we provide," Zadi said, adding that the company had a renewable 15 year contract with the government.
"We're responsible for the management, the energy policy of Ivory Coast is not down to us. That's the role of the state."
Turnover in the 1994-95 financial year (ends September 30 1995) was 130.4 billion CFA francs compared to 102.4 billion CFA in the 1993-94 financial year.
After-tax profit in 1994-95 was just under 2.2 billion CFA against just over 1.8 billion CFA in 1993-94, an increase of 19.6 percent.
Commenting on the 1995-96 results, Zadi said with a smile: "We have done a little better (than the year before)."
The company, which has about 3,200 staff, was now collecting on 98 percent of bills for its services, he added. Prior to privatisation, the figure was around 60 percent.
Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, has a capacity of around 1,100 megawatts, about half of it from hydroelectric power -- traditionally the mainstay of the sector.
A new gas-fired 100 Megawatt power station came on stream in 1995 at Vridi just outside Abidjan and a second one of a similar size is planned in the outlying suburb of Yopougon.
President Henri Konan Bedie's government has set itself a target of extending power supplies to the country's villages. It also wants to industrialise -- creating further need for power.
Zadi said the challenge was not one of capacity but getting the power to outlying villages in rural areas. "The need is there, its the means that are lacking."
To date, about 1,200 of the 8,500 villages has electricity.
Zadi said the gas was projected to last for over 20 years but that the government was looking to the longer term.

Hydroelectric power looked like the best alternative source of power at present, he added. "If we manage the gas and the hydroelectrics well then we will be able to secure the future generation of electricity," he said.
Ivory Coast's hydroelectric capacity was hard hit by drought and lack of investment in the late 1980s and early 1990s. "With the drought we were obliged to diversify," Zadi said.
At that time, Ivory Coast relied on imports from neighbouring Ghana. Now the roles have reversed.
Ivory Coast began exporting to Ghana in 1995 and along the same line to Benin and Togo. It also supplies a couple of villages just across the border in landlocked Mali.
Zadi said plans to sell electricity to neighbouring Burkina Faso were being studied. At a future date Ivory Coast could supply more of Mali and even border areas in Guinea, he added.
Zadi said that the advent of gas had brought production costs down dramatically but he said it was too early to talk of large price cuts to industrial or domestic consumers.
He said the initial aim was to enable the sector to pay its way. "If they privatised it was to clean up the sector."
